newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries end higher on foreign, index buying.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries end higher on foreign, index buying.

text.p: U.S. Treasuries ended higher for the second straight day on Friday, aided by improving technical factors and hopes the economy will continue to show moderation in the second quarter.

Once again, the market was boosted by heavy foreign activity, which included Asian purchases of intermediate-term securities and long bonds, and European buying at the shorter end of the curve, analysts said.
Treasuries gained momentum as the session went on and yields ended at their lowest levels in more than a week.
The 30-year bond closed at 96-10/32, up 23/32 from Thursday, while its yield dove to 6.92 percent from 6.98 percent. In two sessions, the bond yield fell 11 basis points.
Meanwhile, the two-year note was down 5/32 to 100-2/32, with its yield falling to 6.22 percent from 6.30 percent.
Like its long-end counterpart, the two-year's yield retraced to levels not seen since May 20, the day the Federal Reserve chose to leave interest rates steady.
Treasuries, though, closed off their best levels of the session on a bout of light profit-taking late in the day.
Still, "There's a much better feel to the market than a few days ago," said Jim Nealis, head bond trader at PaineWebber Inc. "The selling from hedge funds we had seen a week ago has disappeared."

Helping the market most, Nealis said, was the resetting of major bond indexes, such as those from Lehman Brothers and Salomon Brothers. "To maintain their indexes (many accounts) had to buy today," he said.
Players also cited the release of benchmark revisions to the monthly employment report as another key factor, as the market now expected non-farm payrolls estimates to be lowered.
Economists reduced forecasts for May payrolls -- which will be released next Friday -- by as much as 100,000 to totals below 200,000.
"That gave a bid to the market," said Kevin Flanagan, money market economist at Dean Witter Reynolds Inc.
Another factor that helped the short end, market participants said, was continued asset allocation shifts from stocks into bonds.
Early in the session, the Dow Jones industrials were down as much as 80 points, before staging a late-day rally. The Dow closed up an unofficial four points.
Analysts said stock investors became wary after computer chip maker Intel warned that second-quarter revenues and profits would fall short of expectations.
That led to a so-called flight-to-quality into an already expensive front end.
Technical factors overshadowed a number of economic releases on Friday morning, which were described as mixed.
First, the Commerce Department revised first-quarter growth upwards to a 5.8 percent growth rate from the initially reported 5.6 percent -- below expectations for a rate of 6.0 percent or higher.
Second, Commerce reported a 7.7 percent decline in April single-family home sales to a 772,000 annual unit rate, its largest monthly drop since October.

Also, the University of Michigan's May consumer sentiment index rose to 103.2 from 101.4 in April, and Chicago Purchasing Managers reported their business barometer fell to 56.8 in May versus 57.2 in April. But, its prices paid index jumped to 56.9 from 53.3.
Some players expressed concern the National Association of Purchasing Management May prices paid index might show similar gains in prices.

Early in the day, activity was dominated by foriegners, bailing out of European bonds and heading for Treasuries. There were also reports of large Asian funds buying blocks of 10-year and 30-year Treasuries.

Players said nerves over the possibilty of a socialist goverment in France in the wake of this Sunday's election, uncertainty over the Euro and the continued dispute between the German government and the Bundesbank over gold revaulation sparked the renwed foreign interest into U.S. Treasuries.
Bill rates continued to perform the best on the yield curve, but dealers said the low supply of bills was keeping rates low.

The three-month Treasury bill rate closed down eight basis points points at 4.82 percent. The six-month bill rate fell two basis points to 5.19 percent. The year bill rate was down six basis points at 5.46 percent.
The five-year note traded up 13/32 at 99-31/32 to yield 6.52 percent. The 10-year note closed up 18/32 at 99-23/32, yielding 6.67 percent.
